sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Existing multi-agent collaboration (MAC) methods have primarily explored a group thinking collaboration topology, where agents independently generate solutions and aggregate their outputs. In this work, we investigate an alternative relay thinking topology, where reasoning ownership is dynamically transferred across agents, allowing subsequent agents to inherit and refine an evolving reasoning trajectory. We introduce Multi-Agent Confidence-guided Relay (MACR), a framework that enables dynamical relay collaboration among agents. The key challenge is determining when reasoning should be relayed and which agent should continue the process. method addresses this challenge through confidence-guided relay triggering and a bidding mechanism that selects the next agent based on its confidence. Experiments on four benchmarks show that method outperforms the strongest single-model strategies in accuracy, e.g., +3.3% on MathVista and +3.9% on MMStar, and remains on par with multi-agent strategies while consuming 6.0x less token overhead on HallusionBench and MMStar. Further analysis demonstrates that relay collaboration enables heterogeneous agents to progressively integrate complementary insights, combining heterogeneous capabilities across reasoning stages. Our source code is available at https://github.com/67L1/MACR.

sections.title: ABSTRACT
sections.content: Existing multi-agent collaboration (MAC) methods have primarily explored group thinking collaboration topology, where agents independently generate solutions and aggregate their outputs. In this work, we investigate an alternative relay thinking topology, where reasoning ownership is dynamically transferred across agents, allowing subsequent agents to inherit and refine an evolving reasoning trajectory. We introduce Multi-Agent Confidence-guided Relay (MACR), framework that enables dynamical relay collaboration among agents. The key challenge is determining when reasoning should be relayed and which agent should continue the process. MACR addresses this challenge through confidence-guided relay triggering and bidding mechanism that selects the next agent based on its confidence. Experiments on four benchmarks show that MACR outperforms the strongest single-model strategies in accuracy, e.g., +3.3% on MathVista and +3.9% on MMStar, and remains on par with multi-agent strategies while consuming 6.0 less token overhead on HallusionBench and MMStar. Further analysis demonstrates that relay collaboration enables heterogeneous agents to progressively integrate complementary insights, combining heterogeneous capabilities across reasoning stages. Our source code is available at GitHub.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Background. Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate impressive reasoning capabilities (Zhang et al., 2025a; Xu et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026c). However, when solving complex problems, single model might encounter intermediate reasoning bottlenecks that limit further progress (Shojaee et al., 2026; Yan et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026b). Multi-Agent Collaboration (MAC) has emerged as an effective approach to address such challenges by enabling multiple models to interact and exploit complementary capabilities (Jin et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025b; Bajoria et al., 2026; Tran et al., 2025; Ferrag et al., 2026; Abou Ali et al., 2025; Gupta et al., 2025). Existing studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of MAC in various domains, e.g., mathematical reasoning (Qian et al., 2025; Davoudi et al., 2025), visual question answering (Wang et al., 2026c;a), and multi-step decision making (Weng et al., 2025; Nourzad et al., 2025). Motivation. Despite their diversity, most MAC methods follow group thinking collaboration pattern (Janis, 1982), where multiple agents contribute reasoning trajectories in parallel and integrate information through interaction or aggregation (Li et al., 2024; Veluri et al., 2024; Becker et al., 2026) (cf. Fig. 1a). This pattern enables agents to contribute parallel perspectives and reach synthesized solution. However, collaboration among intelligent systems can take multiple forms. Cognitive science Figure 1: Comparison of group thinking and relay thinking in MAC. Equal contribution. Corresponding author.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Figure 2: KDE of local confidence across three models, before (a) and after (b) calibration. suggests another pattern of collective problem solving, referred to as relay thinking (Michael, 1998; Van Eeckhout et al., 2025), where one participant develops an intermediate idea and transfers it to another participant for further refinement. Inspired by this sequential knowledge transfer process, we explore relay-style collaboration topology for MAC, where agents progressively inherit and extend shared reasoning trajectory through sequential ownership transitions (cf. Fig. 1b). Methodology. Realizing relay collaboration requires addressing two questions: when should reasoning ownership be transferred, and which agent should continue the reasoning process. We use model confidence as signal for these decisions, motivated by previous studies showing that confidence estimates can provide information about reasoning reliability (Xu et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b; Farquhar et al., 2024). Moreover, we also observe in Fig. 4 that correct and incorrect trajectories are separable in confidence. However, confidence values derived from heterogeneous models are not directly comparable due to differences in model architectures, vocabulary spaces, and probability distributions (cf. Fig. 2). To address this, we propose the Multi-Agent Confidence-guided Relay (MACR). MACR begins by extracting local confidence across heterogeneous model pool using sliding window for confidence calibration, reducing the Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) value from 13.31 to 1.01 (cf. Fig. 2). On this basis of comparable confidence across heterogeneous models, MACR monitors the leading models calibrated confidence and interrupts generation to initiate bidding once that model shows low confidence, relaying generation rights to the model with the highest confidence. Besides deciding when and to whom to relay, MACR must also determine which model should start the task. To this end, it initializes the leading model via an initial bidding round, selecting the model with the highest calibrated confidence to start the task. These steps together constitute MACRs online initiationmonitoringbiddingrelay loop (cf. Fig. 3). Contributions. First, we offer new perspective on MAC patterns by drawing on relay thinking, where reasoning trajectory is progressively refined and synthesized as it is relayed across heterogeneous models. Second, we develop MACR, confidence-guided relay framework that calibrates confidence across heterogeneous models and jointly determines model initiation and reasoning handoffs through bidding. Third, we reveal two empirical properties underlying effective heterogeneous collaboration: models exhibit complementary strengths across reasoning stages, while reasoning bottlenecks emerge at different stages across tasks. We hope these findings motivate dynamic model scheduling that adapts both reasoning ownership and relay timing throughout inference. Results and Analysis. Experiments on four multimodal benchmarks show that MACR outperforms single-model strategies in accuracy, e.g., +3.3% on MathVista and +3.9% on MMStar, and remains on par with multi-agent strategies while consuming 6.0 fewer tokens on HallusionBench and MMStar, respectively. Qualitative analysis reveals that MACR integrates the isolated cues of single models into global reasoning chain(cf. 3.3). Furthermore, our analyses confirm that heterogeneous models in MACR are complementary, both across their capabilities (cf. Fig. 6a) and across reasoning stages(cf. Fig. 6b), and that they are capable of localizing task-agnostic bottlenecks(cf. Fig. 6c).

sections.title: 2 METHODOLOGY
sections.content: MACR requires determining two things. First, it requires the real-time identification of local reasoning bottlenecks. While models logarithmic probabilities indicate its confidence, we find that their confidence is incomparable. Therefore, models confidence needs calibration to enable cross-model bidding. Second, it must evaluate which candidate model is best suited to take over generation. Candidate models perform short trial generations on shared context, and MACR evaluates their confidence under the calibrated metric to execute handovers.

sections.title:
3 EXPERIMENT
3.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
Datasets. To evaluate MACR across diverse dimensions, we adopt four benchmarks. MMStar (Chen
et al., 2024) evaluates comprehensive multi-modal capabilities across 6 abilities and 18 tasks. Hallu-
sionBench (Guan et al., 2024) diagnoses the visual and knowledge hallucinations. LogicVista (Xiao
et al., 2024) assesses structured reasoning in visual contexts, covering inductive, deductive, numer-
ical, spatial, and causal logic. MathVista (Lu et al., 2024) evaluates joint visual-mathematical
reasoning across geometry, charts, and word problems.
Baselines. We compare MACR against single-model and multi-agent strategies. The model pool
consists of Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct (Yang et al., 2025a), InternVL3.5-8B (Wang et al., 2025b), and
MiniCPM-V-4.5-8B (Yu et al., 2026).
• Single-Model Strategies. We evaluate standard input–output prompting (IO), where the model
directly outputs the solution and answer from the given images and question; CCoT (Mitra et al.,
2024) prompts the LLM to generate a scene graph capturing objects, attributes, and their relation-
ships first, and then uses that scene graph to produce the final response; and DDCoT (Zheng et al.,
2023) decomposes complex problems into actionable sub-tasks and then produces the final answer.
• Multi-Agent Strategies. We benchmark against two multi-agent strategies: Majority Vote
(MV) (Wang et al., 2023), establishing consensus across independent model generations, and
H-DMAD (Liu et al., 2025), a diverse multi-agent collaboration framework that assigns different
reasoning strategies (CoT (Zheng et al., 2023), CCoT, and DDCoT) to different agents, encouraging
complementary perspectives to break the fixed mental set, and fuses their outputs into a final answer.
Implementation Details. We set the sliding window size w = 16 and the confidence threshold τ =
−0.3 via parameter search on 600 randomly sampled instances from RealWorldQA (X.AI, 2024),
which are disjoint from all evaluation sets. All evaluations are conducted under identical settings
(e.g., temperature). To ensure reliability and rule out the influence of generation randomness, we
conduct all evaluations with three distinct random seeds. We report accuracy as the mean ± standard
deviation, and additionally report token usage along with the Incremental Benefit per Cost (IBC),
defined as ∆Acc/∆Tokens relative to each single model’s IO baseline (Aggarwal et al., 2024).
sections.content: 3.2 QUANTITATIVE COMPARISON RESULTS The results demonstrate that MACR consistently surpasses single-model strategies in accuracy while remaining comparable to multi-agent strategies with minimal token overhead (cf. MACR operates with 6.00 fewer tokens on HallusionBench (4,414 vs. 26,375) and MMStar (4,150 vs. 24,677). To quantify the efficiency gain of MACR, we evaluate the IBC (Aggarwal et al., 2024). MACR dominates IBC across all datasets with state-of-the-art IBC of 21.35, e.g., boosting performance by +18.52 on MMStar (21.35 vs. 2.83) and +12.75 on MathVista (15.38 vs. 2.63) over H-DMAD, substantiating that relay thinking successfully maximizes collective intelligence while preventing generation waste. 3.3 QUALITATIVE ANALYSIS We compare MACR reasoning trajectories against those of single-model CoT. In cases where CoT fails (cf. Fig. 5, left), single models anchor on isolated cues (e.g., local textures or lighting attributes), whereas MACR succeeds by synthesizing these fragmented cues into more comprehensive global view. This advantage extends to failure cases where both methods produce an incorrect answer (cf. Fig. 5, right). Even then, MACR still attempts comprehensive integration, whereas CoT focuses on an isolated patch. This indicates that MACR enhances the generation quality by executing global contextual integration, even when the underlying model pool reaches its capability ceiling. 3.4 ANALYSIS 3.4.1 CAPABILITY ROUTING ANALYSIS To validate the necessity of bidding, we analyze the cross-model transition matrix (cf. Fig. 6a). The row-normalized transition probabilities reveal bidirectional relay dynamics. While MiniCPM-V 4.5 has the highest self-transition rate (59.7%), it still yields dominance to InternVL 3.5 or Qwen3 VL in 40.3% of its bids. Furthermore, bidirectional exchanges between peers are frequent. InternVL 3.5 transfers to Qwen3 VL (22.4%), while Qwen3 VL returns control (26.9%). This indicates that no single model maintains absolute dominance. Instead, it demonstrates that they complement each other. By leveraging calibrated local confidence, MACR matches each bottleneck with its optimal model. Our ablation findings corroborate this complementarity (cf. 3.4.4). 3.4. INFERENCE SURVIVAL ANALYSIS To quantify the continuous generation capability of models, we conduct Kaplan-Meier survival analysis (cf. Fig. 6b). This indicates that models excel at different stages of generation. Unlike traditional turn-based strategies that may either disrupt long-horizon reasoning or cause early-survival models to accumulate hallucinations during later stages, MACR relays generation according to each models stage-wise retention. Consistent with these temporal dynamics, employing punctuation-based fixed triggers degrades performance (cf. 3.4.4). 3.4.3 TASK-AGNOSTIC BOTTLENECK LOCATION ANALYSIS To validate that MACR is task-agnostic, we analyze the distribution of bidding triggers across different tasks (cf. Fig. 6c). The distributions reveal contrasting relay patterns across datasets. While logic-heavy tasks (LogicVista, MathVista) exhibit dense relays in the early stage, visual-intensive tasks (MMStar, HallusionBench) concentrate their relays in later stages. Furthermore, across all tasks, bidding frequency consistently stabilizes during the final stage as models converge on final answers. MACR localizes these task-agnostic bottlenecks, adapting to the unique reasoning paradigms of different domains. If MACR adopts task-blind periodic relays, accuracy degrades (cf. 3.4.4). 3.4.4 ABLATION STUDY To verify the necessity of MACRs initiation, capability matching and bottleneck localization, we ablate the respective modules on 500 randomly sampled instances from MMStar. Initiation. The initial leading model is fixed to each of the three models in turn while keeping the rest of the pipeline unchanged (Fixed Initiation, FI). FI achieves 71.6%, 71.2%, and 70.4% for MiniCPM-V 4.5, InternVL 3.5, and Qwen3 VL, respectively, compared with MACRs 72.4%. sections.title: 3.4.5 ANALYSIS ON MODEL POOL HETEROGENEITY
sections.content: To validate the necessity of diversity within the model pool, we restrict MACRs model pool to single homogeneous model (MiniCPM-V 4.5, InternVL 3.5, or Qwen3 VL) and evaluate two homogeneous multiagent collaboration pattern variants on 500 randomly sampled instances from MMStar (cf. Table 3). Method RPH TDH MACR 68.00 66.60 64.80 63. 70.20 68.80 72.40 Role-Playing Pattern (RPH) prompts single model with three distinct personas: Proponent proposing the initial reasoning and answer, an Opponent formulating rebuttals and alternative perspectives, and Mediator resolving conflicts (Lu & Su, 2026). RPH achieves 68.0%, 70.2%, and 64.8% for MiniCPM-V 4.5, InternVL 3.5, and Qwen3 VL, respectively, compared with MACRs 72.4%. This shows that simulated persona diversity fails to match true architectural complementarity. Table 3: Analysis on model heterogeneity. All results are reported in Acc. (%). Temperature-Decoded Pattern (TDH) simulates intra-model diversity by elevating the sampling temperature during the bidding phase, generating three distinct reasoning paths. The trajectory that maximizes local confidence is then adopted and concatenated to the context. TDH yields 66.6%, 68.8%, and 63.6% for MiniCPM-V 4.5, InternVL 3.5, and Qwen3 VL, underperforming MACR. This shows that sampling strategies cannot substitute for complementary heterogeneity. The results indicate homogeneity leads to performance degradation. Consistent with recent findings (Bertalaniˇc & Fortuna, 2026), homogeneous pools lack intrinsic diversity and thus cannot produce cognitive diversity. Conformity tendency may drive them to converge on flawed consensus. 3.4.6 LEXICAL PROFILING OF REASONING BOTTLENECKS To semantically characterize models reasoning bottlenecks, we analyze the lexical distribution of tokens generated immediately preceding bidding trigger (cf. Fig. 7). The resulting distributions show distinct lexical patterns across models. InternVL predominantly falters around analytical evidence extraction (e.g., analyze, examine, identify), MiniCPM-V around spatial localization and attribute binding (e.g., position, top, left, large), and Qwen3-VL around causal deduction (e.g., since, therefore, suggesting). Despite these differences, all models share universal hesitation signature, frequently outputting stall tokens (e.g., wait, look, check). This lexical heterogeneity aligns with the complementarity we observed (cf. 3.4.1), suggesting that different models tend to hesitate at different stages and motivating MACRs design of matching each bottleneck with its optimal model.

sections.title: 4 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Multi-Agent Debate (MAD) improves performance by leveraging interactions among LLMs. Existing MAD methods are broadly categorized into two streams. The first category is Collaboration Workflow Optimization (Hong et al., 2024; Maiga et al., 2025; Li et al., 2024; Pham et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024; Li et al., 2023; Zhang & Xiong, 2025). These methods structure multi-agent collaboration to resolve tasks, e.g., orchestrating role-based coordination pipelines (Hong et al., 2024; Maiga et al., 2025), communicating via continuous embeddings (Pham et al., 2024), and optimiz-

sections.content: Figure 7: Lexical distribution of three models. ing communication topologies or multi-perspective reward frameworks (Li et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024; Li et al., 2023; Zhang & Xiong, 2025). The second category is Failure Diagnosis and Intervention (Wynn et al., 2025; Yao et al., 2025; Cemri et al., 2026; Choi et al., 2026a; Yang et al., 2025b). These methods diagnose and mitigate collaborative limitations, e.g., quantifying sycophancy and social conformity to prevent premature convergence (Wynn et al., 2025; Yao et al., 2025), establishing taxonomies for system misalignments (Cemri et al., 2026), and delineating theoretical bounds of debate under test-time scaling (Choi et al., 2026a; Yang et al., 2025b). Despite their impressive performance, these methods are all built around the topology of group thinking, where models produce complete responses that are aggregated after generation. Unlike methods relying on rigid debate turns, MACR monitors confidence in real time and relays generation rights to the most confident candidate when model struggles. Uncertainty and Confidence in LLMs provide signals for evaluating confidence and guiding reasoning. These approaches are broadly divided into two main streams. The first category is Uncertainty Quantification and Decomposition (Wang et al., 2025a; Jayasekera et al., 2026; Feng et al., 2025; Amayuelas et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2026c). They decompose and estimate uncertainty to evaluate confidence or trigger behaviors, establishing bounds or benchmarks for uncertainties (Jayasekera et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2025a), inducing uncertainty awareness through query or tuning (Feng et al., 2025; Amayuelas et al., 2024), and extracting token-level logit margins to dynamically trigger interleaved multimodal reasoning (Liu et al., 2026c). The second category is Confidence-Guided Collaboration and Reinforcement (Zhu et al., 2026; Ai et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2026; Pappu et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026a; Choi et al., 2026b; Li et al., 2026b; Liu et al., 2026a; Park et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2026). They manage uncertainty within multi-agent frameworks, e.g., modulating belief updates through confidence scores (Zhu et al., 2026; Ai et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2026), mitigating behavioral uncertainties like hallucination, compromise, or bias during debates (Pappu et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026a; Choi et al., 2026b; Li et al., 2026b), and optimizing collaborative policies via translating confidence into reward signals (Liu et al., 2026a; Park et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2026). Despite quantifying uncertainties and optimizing collaborative policies, these methods evaluate sequencelevel outputs and overlook the comparability of confidence across heterogeneous models. Unlike these methods, we first identify the incomparability of confidence across heterogeneous models and provide calibration method for it. Building on this, MACR calibrates local confidence at the window level rather than sequence level, monitoring mid-generation uncertainty and executing cross-model relays the moment local reasoning bottleneck is detected.

sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We introduce MACR, transitioning multi-agent collaboration from group thinking mode to relay thinking mode. Addressing incomparable confidence across heterogeneous models, MACR calibrates local confidence, enabling real-time cross-model bidding. Monitoring the leading model, MACR interrupts generation upon detecting reasoning bottlenecks, transferring generation rights to the most confident model. Experiments across four multi-modal benchmarks demonstrate that MACR outperforms all existing single-model baselines in accuracy, while achieving results comparable to existing multi-agent baselines with 6.0 less token overhead. Further analyses verify that this relay mechanism integrates isolated cues into comprehensive global reasoning chains and exploits model complementarity, with task-agnostic selection mechanism.
